# Test fixtures

Every other test in this crate synthesizes its bytes in Rust. An Ogg Opus
stream can't be hand-built without an encoder, so this directory is the
exception: the file is checked in, and the command that made it lives here so
it can be regenerated byte for byte.

## tone-440.opus

One second of a 440 Hz sine, 48 kHz stereo, at 64 kbit/s. It's a quiet tone,
around -21 dBFS peak, because that's where lavfi's sine generator sits; the
decode tests bracket the level rather than expecting full scale.

```
ffmpeg -f lavfi -i "sine=frequency=440:sample_rate=48000:duration=1" -ac 2 -c:a libopus -b:a 64k tone-440.opus
```

The file holds 48960 decoded frames: 312 of encoder pre-skip, 48000 of tone,
and 648 of end padding. That split is what makes it a gapless test rather than
just a decode test. Getting exactly 48000 frames back means both trims landed,
and the pre-skip half is the interesting one because Symphonia's Ogg reader
never signals it.

## dense-transients.opus

Two seconds of eight detuned sine partials under a noise burst that retriggers
every 250 ms, 48 kHz stereo at 128 kbit/s, the two channels detuned by a hertz
against each other so they don't collapse to mid. It exists to hold CELT's
time-resolution path open, which the 440 Hz tone above cannot do: a steady sine
never provokes a transient frame, so it never exercises the code that splits a
frame into short blocks.

```
ffmpeg -f lavfi -i "aevalsrc='0.15*sin(2*PI*110*t)+0.15*sin(2*PI*165*t)+0.12*sin(2*PI*220*t)+0.12*sin(2*PI*277*t)+0.1*sin(2*PI*330*t)+0.1*sin(2*PI*440*t)+0.08*sin(2*PI*660*t)+0.08*sin(2*PI*880*t)|0.15*sin(2*PI*111*t)+0.15*sin(2*PI*166*t)+0.12*sin(2*PI*221*t)+0.12*sin(2*PI*278*t)+0.1*sin(2*PI*331*t)+0.1*sin(2*PI*441*t)+0.08*sin(2*PI*661*t)+0.08*sin(2*PI*881*t)':s=48000:d=2" -f lavfi -i "anoisesrc=c=white:r=48000:a=1:d=2:seed=7" -filter_complex "[1:a]volume='exp(-30*mod(t,0.25))':eval=frame,aformat=channel_layouts=stereo[p];[0:a][p]amix=inputs=2:weights=1 1[o]" -map "[o]" -c:a libopus -b:a 128k dense-transients.opus
```

Regenerating gives the same audio but not the same file: ffmpeg picks a random
Ogg serial number per run, so 35 container bytes move while the packet
payloads and the decoded samples come back bit for bit identical. Checked on
ffmpeg 8.1.2. Diff the decoded PCM, not the file, if you ever need to confirm
a regeneration.

The file holds 101 audio packets and decodes to exactly 96000 frames per
channel after the trims, at an RMS near 0.125 and a peak of 0.77.

### What it's guarding

The decoder this crate used before `opus-pure` was `opus-decoder` 0.1.1, which
panics on ordinary music. CELT's anti-collapse mask is one bit per short block,
and that crate accumulated it in a `u8` (`src/celt/vq.rs`) while the block
count reaches 16 once a negative `tf_change` doubles it. `1 << i` for `i >= 8`
then overflows: a panic in debug, and in release the shift amount is masked
instead, so the mask is silently wrong and the anti-collapse never fires where
it should. libopus keeps the same mask in an `unsigned` and only narrows it at
storage.

This is a hard bug to provoke on purpose. It needs a transient frame at 20 ms
(so eight short blocks) *and* a band where the encoder chose `tf_select=1` with
`tf_res=1`, the one combination in the table that yields `tf_change = -1` and
doubles eight to sixteen. Gated noise, drum-like decays, chirps and square
waves all top out at eight blocks no matter the bitrate. Dense tonal content
under repeated broadband transients is what tips it over, which is why the
signal above looks the way it does.

Measured, not assumed: this fixture panics `opus-decoder` 0.1.1 at packet 75 of
101. All fourteen tracks of a real-music corpus panic it too, most inside a
second. `opus-pure` decodes the fixture clean at -68 dB from libopus.

### Why opus-pure

Every pure-Rust Opus decoder on crates.io was put through the same harness:
demux the Ogg to raw packets, decode one packet at a time under `catch_unwind`,
and diff sample by sample against the same file decoded by ffmpeg's libopus.
Error is RMS of the difference relative to RMS of the reference, over fourteen
192 kbit/s tracks. The patched opus-decoder row stops at eight files: at 90x
the decode time it was still grinding hours later, and eight was already enough
to place it.

| crate | result | error vs libopus |
| --- | --- | --- |
| opus-pure 0.2.1 | 14/14 clean | -89 to -126 dB |
| opuscule 0.2.1 | 14/14 clean | -89 to -117 dB |
| ruopus 0.1.2 | 14/14 clean | -89 to -117 dB |
| opus-decoder 0.1.1 + the u8 fix | 8/8 clean, rest not run | -56 to -82 dB |
| opus-rs 0.1.32 | decodes | -18 to -23 dB |
| mousiki 0.2.1 | decodes | -9 to -12 dB |
| opus-wave 3.0.1 | decodes | around 0 dB, output 1.75x too loud |
| rusty-opus 0.9.1 | decodes | silence |
| opus-decoder 0.1.1 | 0/14, panics every file | n/a |

Speed separates them too. Decoding the same two seconds of audio, opus-pure
takes 7 ms and the patched opus-decoder takes 610 ms, about 90x slower, which
is what shipping per-band debug logging in the hot path costs. Both measured in
the same build: optimised, with debug assertions and overflow checks left on,
which is the profile that catches the shift overflow at all.

opus-rs, mousiki, opus-wave and rusty-opus are wrong on their own terms, not
through misuse: each was called the way its own examples and tests call it.
`ropus`, `soundkit-opus` and `opus-embedded` are disqualified before measuring
because they build C (ADR 2).

opus-pure wins on more than the number. It has no dependencies and no build
script, its `unsafe` is all AVX2 and NEON intrinsics behind runtime feature
detection, it decodes into a caller-owned buffer so the decode path never
allocates, it has a real `reset_state` for seeks, and it ships a decoder
conformance suite pinned against libopus 1.6.1 output. Its own test suite,
about 320 tests, passes clean. opuscule and ruopus measured nearly as well but
neither exposes a reset, and ruopus returns a fresh `Vec` per packet.
